items.title: docs: correct code-health marker taxonomy and stale benchmark claims
items.body:
The docs said **25 markers** in eleven places. `biomarkers/registry.py` registers
**49 detectors** (52 marker ids). They are not interchangeable, and collapsing
them to one number both undercounts the work and hides the part that matters:

| Group | Count | Scores into |
|---|---:|---|
| Defect-scoring | 26 | `defect` (8 of them also `maintainability`) |
| Performance | 20 | `performance` only |
| SQL | 3 | `maintainability` only |
| Governance | 3 | nothing — the finding surfaces, the score is untouched |

Only 26 may move the calibrated number, and that restriction is the point, so
the docs now publish the taxonomy rather than a single figure.

`CODE_HEALTH.md` goes from 944 to 533 lines, restructured from a reference
manual into an argument: how a marker is computed (one pure-AST example, one
call-graph example), what each tier is allowed to affect, how the weights were
calibrated, and what the validation does and does not show. The marker roster
and the per-language detector catalogue move to the architecture companion,
which now carries the full roster and the real category membership.

`INTELLIGENCE_LAYERS.md` keeps the five foundational layers and adds the five
that were shipping undocumented: Change Risk, Test Intelligence, Bug History,
Security and Dead Code. Security had no mention anywhere despite having a
full-history scan with introducing-commit attribution.

### Corrections against live code

- refactoring ships six detectors, not five — `extract_method` was missing
- performance covers 11 dialects / 16 language tags, not 5; category cap is 2.0, not 1.0
- hotspots are decayed-churn percentile plus activity floors, not churn x complexity
- bus factor is authors-to-cover-80%, not a >80% ownership flag
- significant commits retains up to 50, not 10
- decisions are mined from five sources, not eight; three were retired
- hooks: the unconditional pre-search injection was removed on purpose; document the nine behaviours that ship
- dead code excludes 17 dynamic patterns, not 4
- drop the Python filesystem precision (87.6%), the Django batchability split and the "11-repo corpus": no supporting data exists in repowise-bench, only in the docs

### Corrections against the benchmark data

- per-repo AUC tops out at 0.86, not 0.90 — the 0.898 figure is a different corpus and weight set
- within-band AUC is 0.525 / 0.572 / 0.593 / 0.718, not "near 0.49", which came from a superseded quartile cut
- band separation is 16.9x raw and 2.18x size-normalized; publish both, since the raw delta is not significant
- state the LOC tie on discrimination and the Popt loss to a prior-defects baseline
- publish the business-impact non-replication: -0.09 against CodeScene's -0.58

### README

Four claims contradicted the repo's own docs and are fixed: the "only
significant result in the field" superlative (BENCHMARKS says all five tools
reach significance on the main run), the 15/15 adoption figure (BENCHMARKS
formally retracts it), "557 cross-function cases" (the real count is ~90), and
`get_why`'s supersession lineage (no decision edges are written today). The
CodeScene licence row said open source; it is proprietary with on-prem Docker.
The headline now leads with the five layers instead of a compression number, the
superseded n=15 agent-loop result is replaced by the n=43 run, and the 135x
default-mode index cost sits next to the 22x.

Marker counts also swept out of `docs/README.md`, `CLI_REFERENCE.md`,
`COMMERCIAL.md`, both plugin skill files, and the three SVG assets that had the
number baked in as text.

### Checks

Internal link and anchor validation passes across all five touched docs,
including the two anchors `docs/architecture/code-health.md` depends on.
Docs-only plus one generator string; no runtime code touched.

### Known gap

`LANGUAGE_SUPPORT.md` says 18 languages; the registry has 19 AST-capable, and
that doc disagrees with itself (13 Full + 4 Good + 1 Partial, then "all twelve"
below the table). Left as-is here rather than fixing one doc and not the
authority doc — worth its own pass.

items.title: chore(npm): drop hardcoded rule count and stale benchmark from the package description
items.body:
The published npm description reads:

> "Open detection standard -- like Sigma, but for AI agents. **751 rules** for prompt injection, tool poisoning, context exfiltration, and MCP attacks. Shipped in Cisco AI Defense. **97.2% recall on NVIDIA garak**."

Both numbers are wrong on the registry right now. The corpus is at 780 on `main` (770 effective), and garak was re-measured to 91.5% on 2026-07-28.

Neither can be kept correct by updating it. The rule count moves most days via auto-crystallize and ecosystem PRs, while the registry description only refreshes on publish — so any number written here is stale between releases by construction. The benchmark has the same problem plus a worse failure mode: a recall figure that drifts upward in a reader's memory while the measured value goes down.

This removes both rather than refreshing them. `data/stats.json` and the README badges stay the place where a current number lives, and they move with the corpus.

Note: the registry listing only changes on the next publish, so this PR fixes the source, not the live description.

items.body:
The README was last substantively updated in #118, two releases ago. It was
missing everything shipped since, and carried one figure that no longer matched
`docs/benchmarks.md`.

## One factual error

The path-hash-index row claimed a smaller hashfile of **"41 vs 73 MiB on the
benchmark tree"**. Neither number appears anywhere in `docs/benchmarks.md`, which
measures **39.7 vs 70.9 MiB** — and that measurement comes from the
larger-than-RAM tree, not the 2.07M-file / ~230 GiB tree the surrounding table
describes. Both the numbers and the attribution are corrected.

The table intro had the same problem in miniature: it said "benchmarked on real
btrfs data (2.07M files, ~230 GiB)" while several rows draw from the other
benchmark. It now names both trees up front.

## Missing since v1.3.0

Each verified present in the tree, not taken from a commit title:

- **Paths beyond `PATH_MAX`** are hashed and deduped rather than skipped (#117, #124, #128)
- **The streaming dedupe pipeline** (#116) — the Stage 2 architecture had no bullet at all
- **The O(extents²) fragmented-file scan fix** (#134)
- **The two dedupe-phase races** — block-hash-search UAF (#123) and the TSAN-found pool lifetime bug (#129)
- **clang ASAN/UBSAN/TSAN CI legs**, warnings-as-errors, and `make check-all` — the CI bullet mentioned only valgrind
- **`--cpu-threads`**, absent from both CLI lists despite being in `--help` and the man page
- **Progress polish**: scan-phase hashing throughput (#120), idle-worker display (#143)

## Consistency and readability

- Dropped the standalone larger-than-RAM `[!NOTE]`. The same ~13× claim appeared
  three times (Why-oans table, that note, "vs upstream duperemove"); its unique
  content — peak RSS and hashfile size — is now a row in the speedups table,
  where the reader is already comparing figures.
- Marked upstream issue references as `upstream #NNN` throughout. Bare `#331`,
  `#374`, `#376`, `#387` now read as oans issues, since oans has its own numbers
  in that range. Matches the style already used for `#396/#407`.

## Checks

All nine internal links resolve; the `#larger-than-ram-dedupe` and
`#what-the-fork-changes` anchors match real headings; and the headline numbers
(~11 min → ~92 s, ~294 → ~188 s, 13.8 vs 179.7 s) were each checked against
`docs/benchmarks.md`.

I did **not** run `scripts/verify.sh`: the diff is markdown-only and touches no
code, so the build/test/valgrind gate has nothing to exercise. Say the word if
you'd rather it ran anyway.

Left alone deliberately, as they look intentional rather than stale: the Debian

items.title: ci(benchmark): Stop auto-updating the README comparison tables
items.body:
### What

Removes the three README auto-update steps from the benchmark workflow. The tables go back to being maintained by hand, which is what their methodology requires.

### Why

The README's benchmark tables are a **same-session** comparison — Abies and Blazor measured on the same machine in the same sitting. That's the only reason the Delta column means anything, and both the README and `blazor-baseline.json` say so:

> Measured with js-framework-benchmark **on the same machine, same session**.

> *"Static baseline — Blazor is not run in CI."*

CI structurally cannot produce a comparable figure. Blazor isn't run there, so the automated update could only swap the Abies column for shared-runner numbers while leaving Blazor's local numbers in place. On its first successful run it did exactly that:

| Benchmark | README (same-session) | CI-generated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create 1,000 rows | 119.5 ms (**+34%** vs Blazor) | 331.8 ms (**+291%**) |
| Create 10,000 rows | 1183.5 ms (**+47%**) | 3342.4 ms (**+336%**) |

Those deltas are the gap between a CI runner and a laptop, published as if the framework had regressed 4×. Merging that would have been worse than publishing nothing — it's a wrong number wearing the authority of automation.

It's the same error as the baseline problem in #341, one layer up: **comparability requires holding the measurement environment fixed.** #341 fixed it for CI-vs-CI; this fixes it for the README's local-vs-local.

### What still works

Nothing of value is lost. CI's valid contribution is Abies measured against its own history:

- the Abies-over-time trend still publishes to `gh-pages`
- the regression gate still compares CI against CI, with the smoothed baseline and 25% threshold from #341
- micro-benchmark throughput/allocation baselines still publish

Only the cross-framework table — which CI was never able to produce honestly — is no longer touched.

### Guardrails against re-adding it

- The reasoning is left **in the workflow** at the point where the steps used to be, with the actual numbers, so the next person sees why rather than re-adding it.
- `scripts/update-readme-benchmarks.py` stays as a local tool and its docstring now opens with **"RUN THIS LOCALLY, NOT IN CI"** plus the failure it causes.
- The README gains a short note that the tables are hand-maintained and why, pointing at the trends page for CI data.

### Follow-up for you

The stale `benchmark/readme-auto-update` branch still exists with that misleading diff on it. Worth deleting so nobody merges it later — say the word and I'll remove it, or delete it from the branches page.

### Testing

- `benchmark.yml` parses; the three README steps are gone (28 steps remain in `benchmark-check`, none matching README).
- No dangling references: nothing in `.github/` or `scripts/` invokes the removed steps.
- `update-readme-benchmarks.py` compiles and `--help` works — still usable locally.

items.title: feat: reverse audit — state-to-context stale dependency detection
items.body:
# PR: Reverse audit — state-to-context verification after compaction

## Blind spot addressed

MemLock's forward audit (`audit_anchors` / `semantic_audit_anchors`) starts
from configured/pinned anchors and asks "did this anchor survive
compaction?". A stored user preference that was never configured as an
anchor is invisible to it. The regression test
`test_forward_only_blind_spot_passes_while_reverse_audit_finds_dependency`
proves the gap: with no anchors configured, forward verification reports
zero drift (`alive_ids=[], drifted_ids=[]`) while `reverse_audit()` finds
the stored material preference `ABSENT` and flags it as a rehydration
candidate.

`reverse_audit()` closes this by starting from **every stored preference**
and asking "is this preference still supported by the active
post-compaction context?".

## What shipped

- `detection.py`: pure, deterministic `reverse_audit(memories, active_region,
  *, now, drift_threshold)` + `reverse_audit_unavailable()` fail-open report.
  Verdicts: `PRESENT / ABSENT / CONTRADICTED / STORED_STALE / AMBIGUOUS /
  UNKNOWN`; structured findings with IDs, evidence, reasons, actions;
  `rehydrate_ids` and `suppressed_ids` lists.
- `__init__.py`: post-compaction reverse pass via a host-supplied preference
  provider (`set_reverse_preference_provider`); `ABSENT + material`
  rehydration candidates merge into the existing priority/slot/char budget;
  provider failure fails open and leaves the turn unchanged.
- `store.py`: optional `reverse` diagnostics on `drift_log` entries.
- `persistence.py`: mnemosyne backend now explicitly raises
  `BackendUnavailableError` instead of silently falling back to FileStore.
- `config.yaml` / `plugin.yaml`: `reverse_audit: false` (disabled by
  default), `reverse_preference_query`, `reverse_limit`; version 0.3.0.
- `docs/REVERSE_AUDIT.md` (new): usage, report interpretation, Mnemosyne
  failure behaviour, forward-vs-reverse distinction, unsupported forms.
  README/ARCHITECTURE/DESIGN updated.
- Tests: `tests/test_reverse_audit_unit.py` (implementation unit tests,
  incl. pre_llm integration + provider-failure), `tests/test_reverse_audit.py`
  + `tests/fixtures/reverse_audit_stale.json` (STALE benchmark suite).

## Contract reconciliation (from t_87076251's 3-pass/5-mismatch report)

1. **Contradiction semantics** — impl now honours
   `metadata.memlock.{preference_key,value}` on active user messages
   (contract §5), not only `key: value` text syntax. Fixture case
   `contradicted-current-context` now returns `CONTRADICTED/suppress`.
2. **Superseded wording** — reason unified to `"stored preference is
   superseded"`, evidence `["superseded_by=<id>"]` (contract §94);
   `STORED_STALE` findings preserve explicit materiality.
3. **ABSENT wording** — unified to the contract-stable
   `"no supporting or contradicting evidence in active context"`.
4. **Error key** — query-failure errors use `reason` consistently across
   the pure function, the boundary harness and the fixture (was split
   `reason`/`message`).
5. **Materiality gap (impl gap flagged)** — kept per contract §100:
   `material` is true only with explicit `standing`/`material` metadata;
   non-tagged stored preferences are reported but never rehydrated. This
   is documented as an intentionally unsupported form.

## Test evidence

- Full suite: **74 passed** (0.13s) — baseline 53 (52 original + 1 new
  drift-log test) + 21 reverse-audit tests.
- STALE benchmark suite: 8/8 cases pass, including the blind-spot
  regression.
- `python3 -m py_compile detection.py __init__.py store.py persistence.py` — OK.
- No unrelated repository changes: diff vs `f6cfb8b` is exactly 15 files
  (4 source, 2 config, 3 docs, 6 test files).

## Intentionally unsupported preference forms

- Semantic-only contradiction (meaning-based, no explicit key/value or
  metadata) → classified `ABSENT`, never `CONTRADICTED` (no LLM judgement).
- Preferences without explicit probes and no derivable keywords → `UNKNOWN`.
- Non-material preferences (no `standing`/`material` metadata) → never
  rehydrated.
- Automatic supersession from recency → never inferred; conflicting live
  values are `AMBIGUOUS`.
- Provider writes — reverse audit never writes/invalidates Mnemosyne.

## Files changed (15)

```
README.md, __init__.py, config.yaml, detection.py, persistence.py,
plugin.yaml, store.py, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/DESIGN.md,
docs/REVERSE_AUDIT.md (new), tests/fixtures/reverse_audit_stale.json,
tests/test_lifecycle.py, tests/test_persistence.py,
tests/test_reverse_audit.py, tests/test_reverse_audit_unit.py (new)
```

items.title: fix(ci): build dist before running benchmarks
items.body:
The Benchmarks workflow crashed on the v1.5.0 release ([run 31267507913](https://github.com/jeremydaly/lambda-api/actions/runs/31267507913)):

```
Error: Cannot find module '/home/runner/work/lambda-api/lambda-api/dist/cjs/index.js'.
Please verify that the package.json has a valid "main" entry
    at Object.<anonymous> (benchmarks/frameworks/lambda-api.js:10:19)
```

## Root cause

`benchmarks/frameworks/lambda-api.js` loads the library from the working tree with `require('../../')`, which resolves through the root package's `main`. #326 changed `main` from `index.js` to `./dist/cjs/index.js`, so the adapter now requires a build — but the workflow only ran `npm ci` inside `benchmarks/`, never installing or building the root package.

The benchmark suite (#327) merged before the dual build (#326), and benchmarks only run on `release: published`, so v1.5.0 was the first time the two met. The `baseline` framework has no lambda-api dependency and completed fine, which is why the log shows 10 green scenarios before the crash.

## Fixes

**1. Build `dist/` before benchmarking.** Adds a root `npm ci --ignore-scripts` + `npm run build` ahead of the benchmark install, matching how `release.yml` sequences the same steps.

**2. Honor `LAMBDA_API_VERSION` in the adapter.** Surfaced while verifying the first fix. `run.js:65` already read the env var, but only for the run metadata that renders the caption — the per-framework table rows use each adapter's own `version` field, and lambda-api's read `package.json` directly. Since that ships a `0.0.0-development` placeholder until publish time, every table row would have rendered as:

```
| lambda-api `0.0.0-development` | 298,049 | ...
```

while the caption directly above it correctly said `lambda-api v1.5.0`. That would have been committed straight into the README by the workflow's final step. The adapter now uses the same `LAMBDA_API_VERSION || pkg.version` precedence as `run.js`.

## Verification

Reproduced locally by deleting `dist/` — same `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at the same adapter line; loads cleanly after `npm run build`.

Ran the exact workflow command end-to-end (`node run.js --md results/RESULTS.md --json results/raw.json --update-readme` with `LAMBDA_API_VERSION=1.5.0`). All 6 frameworks × 10 scenarios complete, and both the caption and every table row now read `1.5.0`. Generated results were reverted out of this branch — the committed numbers should come from the runner, not my laptop.

The subsequent `Format README` step pins `prettier@2`, which matches the repo's `^2.3.2` devDependency, so no version skew there.

## Note

The v1.5.0 README still has stale benchmark numbers, since the workflow never reached its commit step. Once this merges, re-running the workflow via `workflow_dispatch` with version `1.5.0` will refresh it.

16 pages had a breadcrumb, 19 published pages did not, including **all six tutorials** — the pages most likely to be reached directly from a search, and the ones that were orphaned in the first place.

items.title: docs(readme): make the benchmark-image note merge-order-independent (follow-up to #2654)
items.body:
## Why this is a separate PR

**#2654 was merged at `c3dfd2b5` while this commit was still being written**, so `3fc0747c` never landed. This is that one commit, rebased on nothing — its parent `c3dfd2b5` is already an ancestor of `release/v1.0.0`, so the diff here is exactly two lines.

## What

The note #2654 shipped at `README.md:826` flatly asserted **"The image above is stale."** That is true today and becomes **false** the moment the `docs/benchmark.svg` correction lands (#2652, branch `lane-e/claims-gate-2`, commit `1a170806`) — and false in the *worse* direction: a reader who checks the image against the note finds the note wrong, and then discounts the corrected numbers sitting right next to it.

Verified the peer branch's SVG **without merging it**, so the lanes stay independent and the orchestrator can land them in any order:

```
$ git show origin/lane-e/claims-gate-2:docs/benchmark.svg
  >96.4%<   R@5 (482/500)   >1.2 q/s<   harness.py
$ git show origin/release/v1.0.0:docs/benchmark.svg
  >97.0%<   R@5 (485/500)   >232 q/s<
```

`482/500 = 96.4%` and `485/500 = 97.0%`, both exact — the substitution resolves rather than approximates.

## The fix

I deliberately did **not** write "the image now renders 96.4%". That assertion is false until #2652 merges, and this branch cannot know the merge order; asserting another branch's file contents from here would move the staleness rather than remove it. The note is now a conditional that is true under **every** merge order:

```diff
-> **The image above is stale.** `docs/benchmark.svg` is regenerated separately and still
-> renders the retired shadow-harness figures (97.0% R@5 / 232 q/s) …
+> **The table and prose in this section are the published numbers.** If the image above
+> shows **97.0% R@5** or **232 q/s**, you are looking at a stale render of
+> `docs/benchmark.svg` — neither figure was produced by the shipped binary; both came
+> from Python shadow harnesses. The binary-faithful keyword row is **96.4% R@5**
+> (482/500) at **1.2 q/s** (`harness.py`).
```

- **SVG still stale** → the conditional fires, the reader is warned, and the correct values are right there.
- **SVG already fixed** → the conditional does not fire, and every remaining sentence is still true.

Deleting the note was the other option on the table and was rejected: an absent note cannot go stale, but it also cannot stop a reader from trusting a headline overclaim rendered **as pixels** — which is the exact failure this note exists to prevent. A conditional gets the safety without the blind spot.

The matching `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` sentence is updated to describe the note as merge-order-independent and to say why.

## Scope

`docs/benchmark.svg` is **not** touched here — it is #2652's surface. Two files, two lines.

Docs-only; `paths-ignore` will skip most of the matrix. Gates run locally: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `bash scripts/check-docs-vs-ssot.sh` (**PASS** — schema=88, full_tools=103, routes=94, paths=80, cli 89/91, mem_fields=30, release=1.0.0), `bash scripts/check-hardcoded-literals.sh` (**PASS**).

items.title: fix: make TransformerForge tracing opt-in and harden API input
items.body:
## Summary

Replaces TransformerForge's badge-heavy, claim-led README with an evidence-led project guide and hardens the FastAPI inference boundary.

## Problem

Importing the API configured an OTLP exporter to `localhost:4318` even when no collector was configured. This produced background connection-refused errors during normal local tests and startup. The request model also silently ignored unknown JSON fields, making unsupported client controls appear accepted.

The README amplified unsupported claims through a large static badge block and stale benchmark/coverage figures.

## Root cause

Tracing treated a local collector as an implicit default instead of an explicit deployment dependency. Pydantic's default extra-field behavior was left unchanged. The README presented static, self-asserted badges and historical measurements without centering their scope or reproducibility.

## Changes

- Configure OpenTelemetry only when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is explicitly set.
- Reject undeclared fields in `POST /summarize` requests.
- Add regression tests for both behaviors.
- Replace the badge wall with live CI and license badges.
- Document the actual lightweight/full modes, API contract, architecture, configuration, verification commands, measured-boundary caveats, security boundaries, and limitations.

## Engineering rationale

Opt-in tracing avoids surprising network activity in local and CI environments while preserving observability for deployments that configure a collector. Rejecting unknown fields makes the public API contract fail closed. The README now points to reproducible commands and implementation paths rather than treating static badges as proof of capability.

## Validation

- `python -m pytest -q tests/test_api.py` with `TRANSFORMERFORGE_LIGHTWEIGHT_MODE=true`
  - Result: `9 passed in 0.37s`
- `python benchmarks/benchmark_lightweight.py` with `TRANSFORMERFORGE_LIGHTWEIGHT_MODE=true`
  - Result: completed and wrote JSON/Markdown benchmark artifacts (Windows 11, CPython 3.12.13).
- `ruff check src/python/inference.py tests/test_api.py`
  - Result: all checks passed.
- `git diff --check`
  - Result: passed.

The full optional transformer/RAG runtime was intentionally not exercised: it can download models and requires the separate `requirements-llm.txt` dependency set.

## Risk

Low. Deployments that intended to export OTLP traces must now set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` explicitly. Requests containing unsupported JSON fields now receive a 422 response instead of having those fields ignored.

## Rollback

Revert this PR to restore the prior tracing default, request parsing behavior, and README.

## Follow-up work

- Pin and verify third-party GitHub Actions before treating security automation as a release gate.
- Evaluate full transformer and RAG paths with versioned datasets and task-specific quality metrics.
